title: Utilising a novel surveillance system to enhance field screening activities for the leishmaniases
author: Panahi, Shivas, et al.

steps.title: Prepare honey‑dye mixture
steps.instruction: In a 50 mL tube combine 100 % pure honey with blue food dye at an 80:1 (honey:dye) volume ratio (e.g., 80 mL honey to 1 mL dye) and mix by inverting several times or using a wooden applicator stick until homogeneous. Ensure the final volume is sufficient to coat all cards. Omit the dye if it is not required.

steps.title: Cut FTA cards to size
steps.instruction: While wearing laboratory gloves, cut each FTA® Classic Card (Cat#WB120205) into 2.5 cm × 2.5 cm pieces (or any preferred dimensions). Sterile conditions are not necessary.

steps.title: Apply honey mixture to cards
steps.instruction: Place the cut cards on Parafilm (or similar) and, using a disposable Pasteur pipette, add 0.5–1 mL of the honey (or honey‑dye) mixture onto each card. Distribute the mixture evenly with the pipette tip; if the mixture is too viscous, trim the pipette tip to facilitate coating.

steps.title: Dry coated cards
steps.instruction: Allow the honey‑coated cards to sit at room temperature for 24–48 h so the honey absorbs evenly. If ambient humidity exceeds 90 %, extend the drying time to 48–72 h.

steps.title: Store coated cards before use
steps.instruction: Place each honey‑coated card in a plastic resealable bag together with 2–4 silica beads to absorb moisture until the cards are deployed in the field.

steps.title: Field deployment and post‑collection storage
steps.instruction: Use the honey‑coated cards in appropriate insect catch containers as described elsewhere. After field collection, return each card to a resealable bag with 2–4 silica beads for storage.

description: FTAⓇ cards are coated in honey to feed biting insects and collect their saliva. Cards can then be processed to detect insect-borne pathogens by preserving nucleic acid (DNA and RNA) [1]. Additionally, blue dye is added to the honey, to provide evidence of feeding on inspection of insects. If this is not required, then omit the blue dye. Alternative sugar sources such as glucose, fructose, trehalose, etc. could potentially substitute honey however, they have not been trialled in this study.
